document_title: The Every-day Life of Abraham Lincoln: A Narrative And Descriptive Biography With Pen-Pictures And Personal; Recollections By Those Who Knew Him
author: Francis F. Browne
claims: The Gettysburg Address was delivered at the dedication of the National Cemetery at Gettysburg.
The address is described as Lincoln's most eloquent and touching public appeal, possibly second only to the Gettysburg oration.
Gladstone of England commented on the address, seeing in it the effect of sharp trial to raise men to a higher level of thought and action.
Gladstone stated that Lincoln's words showed that anxiety and sorrow had wrought their true effect upon him.
The address begins by referencing the nation's founding fathers who brought forth a new nation conceived in liberty and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.
The address acknowledges the ongoing Civil War as a test of whether a nation conceived in liberty can endure.
The address calls for the living to dedicate themselves to the unfinished work of those who fought at Gettysburg.
The address expresses the hope that the nation shall have a new birth of freedom.
The address articulates the concept of government of the people, by the people, for the people, and states it shall not perish from the earth.
The address contains phrases such as 'The fiery trial through which we pass will light us down, in honor or dishonor, to the latest generation.'
The address asserts that 'We say we are for the Union. The world will not forget that we say this.'
The address states, 'We know how to save the Union. The world knows we do know how to save it.'
The address declares, 'We--even we here--hold the power and bear the responsibility.'
The address links the assurance of freedom for the free to giving freedom to the slave.
The address states, 'We shall nobly save, or meanly lose, the last best hope of earth.'
The address suggests a way that is 'plain, peaceful, generous, just--a way which, if followed, the world will forever applaud, and God must forever bless.'
The Gettysburg Address was rewritten many times.
The Gettysburg Address is considered the world's model.
The text of the Gettysburg Address is found on pages 512-515.
There is an appreciation of Lincoln's Gettysburg Address mentioned on page 513.
The Gettysburg dedication is mentioned on pages 512-515.
